subject: Biology
title: How Hearing Works
description: A fast breakdown of How Hearing Works for builders.

hook.text: Sound is vibration. Your ear turns those vibrations into electrical signals your brain can read.

buildup.text: Sound waves travel through the ear canal and vibrate the eardrum, which shakes three tiny bones.

discovery.text: The cochlea in the inner ear converts vibrations into nerve impulses using 15,000 hair cells.

twist.text: Damaged hair cells never regrow. Loud music destroys them permanently.

climax.text: Cochlear implants bypass damaged hair cells, sending electrical signals directly to the auditory nerve.

punchline.text: Sound is just air vibrating. Your brain makes it music.

quiz.question: Why is hearing loss from loud noise permanent?
options: Damaged hair cells in the cochlea don't regrow

details.summary: Hearing begins when sound waves enter the ear canal, vibrate the eardrum and ossicles, and create fluid waves in the cochlea. Hair cells in the cochlea convert these mechanical vibrations into electrical signals that travel via the auditory nerve to the brain.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding hearing mechanics explains why loud noise causes irreversible damage, how cochlear implants restore hearing, and why age-related hearing loss progresses from high to low frequencies.
takeaways: Sound waves are converted to mechanical vibrations by the eardrum and ossicles
Hair cells in the cochlea transduce vibrations into electrical nerve signals
Damaged hair cells do not regenerate, making noise-induced hearing loss permanent

faq.question: Why is loud noise permanently damaging to hearing?
faq.answer: Intense sound overstimulates and destroys the delicate hair cells in the cochlea. Unlike birds and fish, mammals cannot regenerate hair cells once they are lost. Each exposure to excessive noise permanently reduces hearing capacity.

faq.question: How do cochlear implants work?
faq.answer: Cochlear implants bypass damaged hair cells entirely. An external microphone captures sound, a processor converts it to electrical patterns, and an implanted electrode array directly stimulates the auditory nerve, creating the perception of sound.
